items.title: The Biblical Roots of Love
items.summary: Wierzbicka argues that the Gospel of John helped give European languages a broad sense of interpersonal love. Reading the foot-washing and the Good Samaritan together, she distinguishes reciprocal everyday care among people who know one another from aid to a stranger in crisis.

items.title: What “I Love You” Really Means
items.summary: English groups several relationships under one broad verb, whereas some languages use different terms. Her five-part account of loving a person includes knowing them, thinking of them often, feeling something when thinking of them, feeling tenderness and strongly wanting to do good for them.

items.title: Long-term Love Dynamics in Intercultural Couples in Denmark
items.summary: Two Danish–South Asian couples show how recognising racism, negotiating differences and drawing on practical support can sustain long-term love. The authors treat cultural difference as an opportunity for growth as well as a source of strain.

items.title: The Role of Social Network Sites in Romantic Relationships
items.authors: Manuel Faggiano; Ariela Francesca Pagani; Dominik Schoebi; Silvia Donato
items.summary: A review of 64 studies finds that the effect of social media depends on the behaviour and context. Affection, maintenance and disclosure work differently from surveillance and conflict. The authors call for more diverse samples and stronger designs.

items.title: Ambivalent Terms of Endearment in Latino Romantic Relationships
items.authors: Jacqueline Lechuga; Kyle M. Nabb; Jessica Bray; Michael Zárate
items.summary: Calling a partner tóxico or tóxica can be affectionate while invoking controlling behaviour. Its use was associated with a history of abusive relationships in exploratory analyses. The study could not establish direction of causation.

items.title: Seven Components of Meta-capacity to Love
items.summary: Extending Erich Fromm, the researchers propose a higher-order ability to cultivate and sustain loving relationships. Their literature review and interviews identify seven capacities, including care, respect, responsibility, knowledge and trust.

items.title: Distrustful Intimacies and Dating in Post-Catastrophe Hatay, Türkiye
items.summary: Post-earthquake interviews show how displacement, family surveillance and reduced social space can make young singles wary of forming relationships. Distrust protects people from perceived risk while narrowing opportunities for intimacy.

items.title: What Makes People in Spain Feel Loved?
items.authors: Jaymes Rombaoa; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Zita Oravecz; Saida Heshmati
items.summary: The Spanish sample shared a model of everyday felt love. Warmth, concrete care and family affection were strong signals. Intrusive control generally felt unloving, although interpretation depended on motive and closeness.

items.title: Love Styles, Romantic Beliefs and Dysfunctional Relationship Beliefs
items.summary: In a cross-sectional sample of 604 people, passionate eros and possessive mania correlated with romantic idealisation. Other styles showed different patterns with dysfunctional beliefs, supporting the value of distinguishing love styles.

items.title: Is Romantic Love Universal? Is Romantic Love Innate?
items.summary: Delannoy challenges the inference that romantic love is an automatically triggered biological adaptation. He proposes that stories and social learning help cultivate it, potentially recruiting capacities associated with early attachment.

items.title: How Divorce Rituals Balance Romantic Autonomy and Enduring Commitment
items.summary: Hungarian divorce rituals give couples and communities ways to mark an ending. Balatonyi argues that rituals around both entry and exit can preserve the cultural standing of marriage while recognising freedom to leave.

items.title: Daily Connectedness and Felt Love in Three Family Dyads
items.summary: Daily diary data show that felt love and connectedness move together across family dyads. Timing and direction differ by relationship. For example, how connected parents felt to adolescents predicted parents’ felt love the following day.

items.title: Psychometric Validation of the Parental Love Scale
items.authors: Yichun Liu; Yuan Zhang; Mengya Xia
items.summary: An 11-item scale captures three dimensions of felt parental love: positive responsiveness, authentic connection and stability. Scores correlated with adolescent happiness and life satisfaction and inversely with anxiety and depression.

items.title: Emerging Adults’ Autonomy in Romantic Relationships
items.authors: Victoria Yerofeyeva; Alexandra Bochaver; Ekaterina Tsyganova
items.summary: Young adults often recalled early relationship choices as emotionally driven. Break-up accounts more often incorporated deliberate reasoning. Some who had never dated framed remaining single as an active choice linked to other priorities.

items.title: From Dyadic Exchange to Artificial Companionship
items.summary: Artificial companions and digitally mediated disclosure challenge the assumption that intimacy requires mutual responsiveness. Blair asks whether felt intimacy can be unilateral and whether AI companionship might ease loneliness or deepen isolation.

items.title: Hybrid-working Couples and Home Workspace Boundaries
items.summary: A shared home workspace shapes role boundaries, access to space and power. Couples actively negotiate these arrangements. Sharing a profession can improve mutual understanding while making it easier for work and home boundaries to blur.

items.title: Validation of the Whole Self-Love Scale
items.authors: Katy Sine; Julianne Holt-Lunstad; Wendy Birmingham
items.summary: Whole self-love was associated with life satisfaction, balanced affect and social connection, and inversely with loneliness. The scale showed a weak negative association with narcissism, supporting its usefulness as a distinct measure.

items.title: Buying Love: Why Chinese Women Embrace Male-Coded Game Characters
items.summary: Romance games offer some Chinese women a space to explore emotional availability, equality and idealised intimacy. Zhou connects spending on virtual romance to a gap between these ideals and conventional expectations of men in offline relationships.

items.title: How In-Laws Reshape Adult Sibling Bonds
items.summary: New in-laws can revive childhood sibling roles and renegotiate loyalties. Greater emotional differentiation was associated with closer communication and better conflict management, while unresolved favouritism or hierarchy could intensify exclusion.

items.title: Loving the Stranger Begins Within Oneself
items.summary: Reading Leviticus through Jung and Fromm, Surielow treats care for oneself as a standard for welcoming strangers. She argues that coming to terms with disowned aspects of oneself can reduce projection onto others.

items.title: Parasocial and Real-Life Romantic Love: Experience and Brain Activity
items.summary: Real-life beloveds drew stronger self-reported attachment. Both real and parasocial beloveds drew greater sustained attention than friends or strangers, and parasocial cues drew stronger early automatic attention in this preliminary study.

items.title: Those Who Love Singlehood
items.authors: Elina Moreno; Yuthika Girme; Ana Burik; Sarah Stanton
items.summary: Seeing single life as a chance to grow predicted self-expanding experiences and several wellbeing outcomes. Friends, family and solo activities were important sources of expansion. A novelty exercise produced some short-term benefits.

items.title: Individual Variation in Romantic Love Metaphors in Modern Greek
items.summary: Greek speakers draw on some shared metaphor families while choosing markedly different words and evaluations. The same source domain can express different experiences, making individual usage central to understanding love metaphors.

items.title: Love Metaphors in A Midsummer Night’s Dream
items.summary: Shakespeare reworks familiar embodied metaphors through character, comic situation and poetic invention. The talk uses a small set of examples to show how literary language can extend cognitive accounts of metaphor.

items.title: Comparing Romantic Love and Chocolate Craving
items.summary: Participants who loved someone and craved chocolate reported more craving, pleasure and arousal for their beloved. Attention was more readily drawn towards beloved cues in some analyses, with no clear difference in disengagement.

items.title: Love Against the Grain: Neurodivergent Poetry
items.summary: Krid reads neurodivergent poetry as a record of emotional depth and intimacy on its own terms. Images of uncertainty and attunement to difference challenge assumptions about how love should feel and be communicated.

items.title: Love Metaphors in Indonesian Poetry from the 1960s to the 2000s
items.summary: The study identifies 25 metaphor patterns. Personhood, unity and journey recur prominently. Marpaung highlights unity as a way of conceiving love that shares features with some traditions while varying across others.

items.title: Love Metaphors in the Letters of Eminescu and Kafka
items.summary: Love letters create a space for managing absence, longing and vulnerability. Comparing the two collections reveals shared metaphor patterns as well as differences linked to cultural context and individual experience.

items.title: Benevolent Sexism and Heterosexual Women’s Dating Preferences
items.summary: The study separates warmth or willingness to invest from paternalistic assumptions. It finds some effects of ideological beliefs and responses to undermining behaviour. The talk reports several null effects, including its initial planned benevolence contrast.

items.title: Romantic Love Metaphors in Contemporary Ukrainian
items.summary: Wartime respondents still described romantic love mainly through warmth, home, care and gentle natural phenomena. War imagery was less prominent than anticipated, suggesting that wider cultural and embodied patterns continue to shape metaphor.

items.title: Metaphors We Love By: The Four Loves Revisited
items.summary: A corpus-assisted reading of Greek New Testament usage shows that agapé is conceptualised through multiple patterns, including an object that can be given, a space one inhabits and growth requiring cultivation.

items.title: Mapping Desire in Romantic-Love Discourse and Digital Media
items.summary: Catfishing, ghosting and bodily commodification are treated as settings where platform design, cultural stories and emotion organise desire. Joseph proposes that individual fantasies gain collective force through circulation.

items.title: Love and Intellectualism in Dark Academia
items.summary: In The Secret History, shared intellectual ambition creates intimacy, loyalty and desire while feeding exclusion and destructive obsession. Dark Academia makes overlapping forms of intellectual and romantic attachment visible.

items.title: Disentangling Gratitude and Love Across Cultures
items.summary: Network analysis connects gratitude most directly with pleasure-related wellbeing, whereas love relates to both pleasure and meaning. Cultural setting matters for interpreting these cross-sectional associations and designing follow-up studies.

items.title: A Study of Popular Romantic Fiction Over the Ages
items.summary: Using Ontology Maker to examine romantic fiction across languages, Symons identifies character and conduct as recurring partner-selection criteria. She argues that dating apps for long-term relationships should give these qualities more weight than appearance.

items.title: Family Judgement and Ethnolinguistic Identity
items.summary: Interviews with mixed-language Mumbai families identify food as a particularly salient marker of family judgement. Accent, clothing, religion and caste also influence whether a spouse feels accepted and adopts household practices.

items.title: Intentionality in Bridget Jones’s Diary and Pride and Prejudice
items.summary: Verb patterns depict love in Bridget Jones through perception, communication and active exchange. Austen’s novel places more emphasis on hopes, wishes, admiration and acceptance. The modes of loving depend on the narrative.

items.title: Love in Bulgarian: ОБИЧ and ЛЮБОВ
items.summary: Media examples and a small questionnaire suggest two overlapping Bulgarian love categories. The speaker treats the distinction as a pattern to investigate further, given the size of the sample.

items.title: Cultural Consensus Theory and Love in Daily Life
items.summary: Cultural Consensus Theory measures agreement about which everyday situations make people feel loved. In the US data discussed, compassion and small acts of connection were commonly rated as loving, and monitoring or control as unloving.

items.title: Constructed Love Vocabulary in Historical Sources
items.summary: A Belgian couple’s wartime letters show how threat and separation intensified emotional expression. Their words drew on already familiar Catholic and literary vocabulary, making private feeling a window into shared emotional norms.

items.title: How Culture Creates Sexual Desire and Sexual Love in Early Humans
items.summary: Delannoy advances a historical hypothesis that social experience and the stories people learn help organise sexual and romantic desire. He uses the talk to challenge accounts that treat desire as entirely spontaneous or fixed.

items.title: Romantic and Sexual Desire in the Voice
items.summary: Both kinds of desire used similar vocal cues, including lower pitch and greater breathiness, but sexual desire produced larger departures from neutral speech. Emotional attraction is worth studying alongside physical attraction.

items.title: Love and Loans: Marriage in Pandemic Hungary
items.summary: Hungary’s pandemic marriage rise was publicly attributed to family subsidies. Brides described overlapping motives and usually put love, commitment and family aspirations first while integrating financial and legal advantages.

items.title: Myths of Love in Contemporary Nordic Teenage Series
items.summary: Comparisons between myths and Nordic teenage series reveal recurring narrative patterns behind contemporary screen romances. The parallels are sometimes structural or symbolic, with scope for changes in how stories end and whose love they represent.

items.title: Japanese Audio Erotica Streamers and Parasocial Romance
items.summary: Anime-style imagery, varied content, and selective reciprocity help streamers build audiences and encourage payment. Listeners describe real relaxation and felt intimacy while remaining aware of the performance and fantasy.

items.title: Sex Differences in Romantic Love: An Evolutionary Perspective
items.summary: In the young-adult sample, men reported falling in love sooner and more often. Women reported somewhat greater intensity and preoccupation. The effects were generally small, and the reported commitment difference did not survive adjustment.

items.title: What Counts as Cheating in Romantic Relationships?
items.summary: People place behaviours on a continuum of perceived unfaithfulness, from ordinary social contact to flirting and sex. Judgements vary with personal and relational context, supporting the need to discuss expectations within a relationship.

items.title: Love and Addiction: Subjective Feelings and Brain Responses
items.summary: Participants who were in love and vaped craved their beloved more than vaping and showed stronger early automatic attention to beloved cues. The task identifies specific comparisons and leaves open how far the analogy with addiction extends.

items.title: Emotional Dependence and Relationship Investment
items.summary: Higher perceived investment and longer relationships were weakly associated with lower emotional dependence. The authors suggest emotional dependence should be distinguished from the dependence described by investment theory.

items.title: Changing Love Concepts Among South African Indian Gen X Women
items.summary: Three women’s accounts show that concepts of love change through marriage, divorce and personal development. Duty, service, autonomy and self-worth took on different meanings over their lives.

items.title: Dating After Childhood Abuse
items.summary: Survivors described different ways of approaching trust, bodily autonomy and boundaries. Some used digital contact to control the pace of intimacy, while others found it difficult or unsafe. The study foregrounds individual accounts.

items.title: Can We See Love? Documentary Photography
items.summary: Proximity, gaze, setting and composition help a photograph communicate intimacy. Documentary images can capture fleeting gestures of care and show how social and cultural expectations shape what viewers recognise as love.

items.title: Imagination, Pain and Redemption in Proust
items.summary: Palma argues that Proust’s lovers invest imagined qualities in their beloved, hoping to give life meaning and escape isolation. The gap between imagination and the person generates suffering that can also reveal something about the self.

items.title: Love Motifs in Taíno and Pueblo Art
items.summary: Skoggard interprets motifs in stone, shell and other ritual objects as representations of sexual union, fertility and affection. The reading is an anthropological interpretation of artefacts and their cultural histories.

items.title: Love and Survival Across Systems, Monkeys and Humans
items.authors: Lucia Martin Valverde; Jacob Felipe Badilla Perez
items.summary: The presenters connect primate caregiving and rehabilitation observations with co-regulation. They propose that attachment helps bodies and groups adapt and survive, with implications for how love is conceived across species.

items.title: The Spirituality of Love in Ukrainian
items.summary: Ukrainian idioms blend spiritual ideas about heart and soul with experiences of warmth, movement, vulnerability and proximity. This helps connect general love and romantic love with embodied and religious meaning.

items.title: Love Doesn’t Run Out
items.summary: Experiments found that children and adults usually treated love and trust as less zero-sum than material resources. Perceived renewability helped explain why giving love to one person need not leave less for another.

items.title: There Is No Such Thing as Love: What We Study When We Study Love
items.summary: Researchers study different phenomena under the word love, including internal experience, interpersonal relations and cultural models. Karandashev argues for specifying what is being defined and how it is measured before comparing studies or claiming universality.

items.title: The Felt Love Scale as a Measure of Love as a General Feeling
items.authors: Yuan Zhang; Mengya Xia; Caleb Coates
items.summary: The general felt-love scale showed strong reliability and evidence of validity across two samples. It captures a broader feeling of being loved and is associated with positive and negative wellbeing indicators.

items.title: The Embodied Heart in Cross-linguistic Love Metaphors
items.summary: Languages share embodied patterns such as heat, movement and containment while differing in expressions of what the heart does. The researchers use those patterns to link experience, embodiment and cultural convention.

items.title: Emotional Practices in Polyamorous Relationships in Germany
items.summary: Interviewees described several distinct, incomparable relationships. Commitment often meant loyalty, care and continuity, with companionship, sexuality, cohabitation and parenting combined in different ways. No one partner was expected to meet every need.

items.title: Love and Nation in China
items.summary: Chinese patriotic media use marriage stories to praise service, national unity and model citizenship. Xie argues that apparently private romantic emotion can also be a means of cultivating political identification and gendered duty.

items.title: Love in the Indian Urban Middle Class
items.summary: Urban middle-class couples use the language of romantic choice to present themselves as modern and flexible. Ethnographic cases show how this language can also protect class advantage through exclusion and selective ideas about suitable partners.

items.title: Love in Urban Fantasy with Female Protagonists
items.summary: Selected urban fantasies pair powerful heroines with men who support their leadership, care for children and share practical work. These relationships offer an alternative model of masculinity while retaining action-genre appeal.

items.title: A Multidimensional Model of Love
items.summary: Pinich proposes a model to connect embodied metaphors with worldly, spiritual and imagined versions of love. She uses differences such as real versus idealised love to show how several dimensions can coexist in the concept.

items.title: Intercultural Love in Japanese–Western Marriages
items.summary: Accounts of Japanese–Western couples show how love is practised through ongoing negotiation over communication, intimacy and cultural expectations. Personal relationships also carry wider issues of social positioning and race.

items.title: Baby Makes Three: Marital Love During the Transition to Parenthood
items.summary: Average feelings of love declined moderately across the transition, and roughly half of parents remained stable. Mothers tended to show an earlier decline than fathers, with different factors distinguishing trajectories.

items.title: Skin Colour Among Asian American Speed Daters
items.summary: The study found little overall evidence that Asian American speed daters preferred lighter-skinned partners. A limited pattern appeared for foreign-born women on desirability ratings, without a corresponding effect on date offers.

items.title: Rethinking Love from Nature’s Perspective
items.summary: Kuchta argues for including more-than-human relationships in love research. She proposes that social norms discouraging sensitivity to nature can weaken bonding with the natural world and possibly affect wider relational capacities.

items.title: Representations of the Love Act Across Cultures
items.summary: A preliminary comparison of three cultural settings argues that ritual objects can encode sexual union, fertility, place and group history. Skoggard reads such objects as ways to express and redirect sentiments associated with lovemaking.

items.title: Love in Hausa Language and Culture
items.summary: Hausa expressions for love carry emotional, social, religious and humanitarian meanings. Metaphors of illness or pain can express romantic frustration. The study’s small qualitative sample limits generalisation.

items.title: How Physical Attractiveness and Love Are Related
items.summary: People who report more love tend to rate their partner as more physically attractive. Hill calls this a partner halo effect and distinguishes it from self-rated attractiveness, which is also influenced by self-esteem.

items.title: Love Alamat. Love, Alamat
items.summary: Trinidad uses her experience of Alamat’s fandom to argue that fans experience care as partly reciprocal. Shared humour, everyday Filipino culture and the group’s attention to fans make the attachment feel especially close.

items.title: Phenotypes of Romantic Love
items.summary: Clustering distinguishes mild, moderate, intense and highly sexual profiles of people in love. The profiles vary in relationship and personality characteristics, making variation itself a subject for evolutionary research.

items.title: Romantic Love, Distraction and Task Performance
items.summary: People in love report thinking about their beloved frequently and usually enjoying it. In a task setting, beloved-related information can also divert attention away from what they are trying to do.

items.title: Unspeakable Desires in Mary Dorcey’s When You’re Asleep
items.summary: Dorcey’s representation of maternal love allows affection, guilt, ambivalence and the mother’s subjectivity to coexist. Lens-Fernández locates the transgression in how the relationship is represented.

items.title: Cognitive Poetics of The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
items.summary: Eliot layers metaphors of enclosure, atmosphere and illness to convey hesitation and vulnerability. A cognitive reading helps explain how local imagery constructs the poem’s overall experience of love.

items.title: Fluttering Hearts: Korean Romantic Dramas
items.summary: Korean dramas provide a way to study culturally specific relationship scripts and their appeal to international audiences. Symons proposes that viewers may be drawn to how a shared life is built as much as to the declaration of love.

items.title: Understanding Love in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal
items.summary: Accounts from Tibetan Buddhist nuns suggest that love can be understood through connection, care and belonging even when speakers use different terms. Ford asks researchers to take local concepts seriously when interpreting experience.

items.title: There Is No Happy Love
items.summary: Using poetry and examples including Dante and Beatrice, van Peer examines why literature links love with pain. He questions grand ideals of unconditional love and considers whether more ordinary forms of happy love are possible.

items.title: Do You Really Want a Superior Partner?
items.summary: The wish to admire an exceptional partner can pull against the wish for equality. Ben-Ze’ev argues for giving greater weight to qualities that support shared life, such as kindness and feeling appreciated, while allowing differences between partners.

items.title: Love in Sub-Saharan African Contexts
items.summary: Using South African accounts, Mayer discusses how language, family acceptance, gendered duties, spirituality and self-worth shape love. The presentation emphasises cultural variation and the danger of treating a region as socially uniform.

items.title: Love in the Arab World
items.summary: Arabic poetry and courtly traditions provide historical accounts of passionate love. Fortier argues that medieval Christian and Muslim cultures shared important conventions and raises the possibility of Arabic influence on Western courtly love.

items.title: What’s New with Love in East Asia?
items.summary: Romantic love has become a powerful ideal while remaining intertwined with family approval, status and marriage. Ethnographic cases show how parents and unequal social positions can shape the feasibility of a match.

items.title: Love in China: Politics, Economics and Social Change
items.summary: Wang traces how political ideology, market reforms and contemporary technologies reorganise opportunities for intimacy in China. Cases range from private letters and marriage choices to commercial and artificial companionship.

items.title: Love as a Complex Conceptual Category
items.summary: Love draws on a network of metaphors and related concepts. Kövecses uses cognitive linguistics to connect recurring embodied patterns with variation across kinds of love and cultural settings.

items.title: Why Do I Study Cross-Cultural Semantics?
items.summary: Wierzbicka explains why English emotional vocabulary can distort cross-cultural comparison. She proposes using simpler, widely translatable concepts to describe how different languages organise meanings around love and related emotions.

items.title: Are We a Pair-Bond Species?
items.summary: Fundamentalist polygynous communities provide a setting to examine pair attachment within plural marriage. Jankowiak describes hierarchies and preferences, tensions over exclusive attention and separate forms of idealised love within families.

items.title: Romantic love, culture and environment across 82 countries
items.summary: Reports different associations at individual and national levels: greater intimacy and commitment in more individualistic countries and among people with more collectivist views. Climate indicators also varied with reported love.

items.title: Leonard Cohen: The Duty of Lovers
items.summary: Reads Cohen’s songwriting as a survey of romantic and sexual love in which devotion, spiritual imagery and disillusionment coexist.

items.title: Complex Masculinities of Pop Culture Icons
items.summary: Michael Jackson and Prince challenged narrow ideals of hard masculinity while selectively drawing on racialised and gendered conventions. Shakir examines the space this opened for alternative masculinities.

items.title: Iraqi Yezidi Refugee Marriage Decisions in Germany
items.summary: Connects marriage choices to genocide, displacement and bureaucracy. Romantic and practical love interact with commitments to community and Yezidi continuity.

items.title: Love and Heterotopic Space in Romance Novels Set in Italy
items.summary: Anglophone romances cast Italy as a place where family and tradition enable an apparent journey into the past. These stories make exotic otherness serve the self-image of their Anglo-American protagonists.

items.title: Family Discourse in The Goldbergs
items.summary: Conversational care can take the form of overprotection or intrusion. Rossi tracks how politeness and impoliteness help a parent both involve relatives and assert authority.

items.title: Actional Love and Effective Altruism in Therapy
items.summary: Argues that applied empathy should be complemented with individually tailored practical skills and offers clinical examples of ways to adapt interventions.

items.title: Altruistic Love in International Service-learning
items.summary: Student accounts illustrate how international service-learning can cultivate the practice of giving time and effort for others’ wellbeing without expecting repayment.

items.title: Narcissism and Partner-enhancement
items.summary: Examines whether narcissism changes how people idealise partners over time. Highly narcissistic participants tended to enhance their view of themselves while showing less partner-enhancement.

items.title: Romantic Beliefs in Friends-with-benefits and Romantic Relationships
items.summary: The abstract reports greater jealousy and desire for exclusivity among under-29s in committed relationships than among those in friends-with-benefits arrangements.

items.title: Love in Kahlil Gibran’s The Prophet
items.summary: Analyses Gibran’s use of concrete nouns, dynamic verbs and physical qualities. These stylistic choices make a philosophical vision of love feel active and tangible.

items.title: Maintaining Midlife Love
items.summary: Asks whether sustaining an established relationship can itself be a radical response to expectations of self-reinvention and the tendency to treat partners as replaceable.

items.title: A Philosophy of Wellbeing Account of Love
items.summary: Separates wanting to be with someone from acting for their wellbeing. Explores whether concern for another can be understood in terms of what they value and take pleasure in.

items.title: Causes and Reasons: When Love Is Arational
items.summary: Questions standard accounts of what justifies loving a person. Proposes that lovability depends partly on the responses of the person who loves.

items.title: Care Worker and Child Attachment in Japan
items.summary: Reviews research on sensitivity and responsiveness in early childhood care and calls for closer study of how workers learn attuned, responsive practice.

items.title: Romantic Love and Friendship Love
items.summary: Questions whether sex or sexual attraction is essential to romance and proposes recognising small adult communities organised around shared care, rights and responsibility.

items.title: Paternal Involvement and Parental Relationship Quality
items.summary: Reports an association between fathers’ ratings of their relationship and paternal involvement, including participation in healthcare. The relationship may be mutually reinforcing.

items.title: Adolescent Dating in Southeastern Spain
items.summary: Interviews with education professionals reveal some stereotyped views of Maghrebi and Romani young people’s romances. Recommends intercultural responses tailored to adolescents’ needs.

items.title: Feeding and Intergenerational Bonding in Indigenous Taiwan
items.summary: Research with Tao communities shows how feeding and culturally named emotions organise intergenerational bonds. Funk argues for more culturally specific accounts of attachment.

items.title: Collaborative Autoethnography and Loving Inquiry
items.summary: Proposes that shared inquiry and conditions that make vulnerability feel safe can foster compassion and interpersonal growth in organisations.

items.title: Cultural Variability in Saying I Love You
items.summary: Examines how communities differ in their use, avoidance and interpretation of the declaration, including the role of social norms and non-verbal alternatives.

items.title: Love Dynamics in Academic Exchange
items.summary: Looks at how transnational academic exchanges create relationships that balance autonomy and togetherness and allow partners to make unfamiliar settings meaningful together.

items.title: Romantic Experiences of Autistic and Non-autistic Adults
items.summary: Self-reports point to different experiences, including lower rates of dating and of having been in love among autistic participants. The study centres first-person experiences.

items.title: Home Without Ground
items.summary: Reworks Simon May’s account of love as a search for rootedness. Hoffman argues that loving involves the possibility of making a home together.

items.title: Early Variability in Maternal Sensitivity and Partner Violence
items.summary: Proposes testing whether inconsistent early maternal responsiveness predicts later partner violence beyond average responsiveness, with attachment-related expectations as a possible mechanism.

items.title: Love’s Biological Function and Social Construction
items.summary: Argues that evolutionary or biological explanations of love can coexist with accounts of how institutions and social norms shape particular expressions.

items.title: Agapic Love, Gender Friction and Fertility Decline in South Korea
items.summary: Ethnography connects changing expectations of intimacy and gendered sacrifice with delayed marriage and decisions to seek alternatives to conventional family life.

items.title: Towards a Political Account of Love
items.summary: Draws on Māori aroha to propose that love can guide interpersonal ethics, institutions and policy. The account extends political care to the more-than-human world.

items.title: Romantic-Love Myths and Adolescent Dating Violence
items.summary: Explores educators’ views of how jealousy and aggression are normalised as romance and argues for early detection and education that challenges such myths.

items.title: How Much Does Romantic Rejection Hurt?
items.summary: Experimental feedback produced different subjective and cardiac reactions. Reported hurt peaked under rejection, and depression and neuroticism explained relatively little variation.

items.title: Public Romance, Space and Taste in Urban India
items.summary: Ethnography explores how couples negotiate visibility, safety and respectability across private commercial venues and open public spaces.

items.title: Negotiating Normativity in Experiences of Infidelity
items.summary: Interviews in England show people invoking and resisting competing ideas about monogamy when making sense of infidelity and its place in everyday relationships.

items.title: Commensurable and Incommensurable Love Styles
items.summary: Examines why partners may end a valued relationship to recover autonomy or authenticity and questions how well traditional romantic unity serves contemporary couples.

items.title: Felt Love Dynamics and Flourishing
items.summary: Reports that experiences of felt love appear to persist longer among people with higher flourishing. The association concerns how a feeling carries forward in daily life.

items.title: Receiving Gratitude and Supporting a Partner’s Goals
items.summary: Reports that feeling appreciated predicts motivation to help a partner pursue goals, with special relevance for people with insecure attachment.

items.title: Love and Death
items.summary: Examines how witnessing a death can bring overwhelming love alongside loss. The project compares accounts shaped by Buddhist practice and secular backgrounds.

items.title: Putting God’s Love into Action
items.summary: Follows Danish Pentecostal mission work to ask how participants try to convey divine love across differences in culture and status.

items.title: Romantic Love in Jeanette Winterson’s Early Fiction
items.summary: Shows how Winterson recombines literary conventions, clichés and romance plots to produce queer love stories with overtly interwoven cultural origins.

items.title: Passionate Love, Relationship Satisfaction and Life Satisfaction
items.summary: Among 308 Brazilian adults in committed relationships, passionate love correlated positively with life satisfaction, sexual attraction and affinity of interests. The design leaves causal direction open.

items.title: Do We Implicitly Love Phones and Pets Like Partners?
items.summary: Examines whether positive and negative automatic evaluations coexist for pets and phones as they do for close people. The abstract describes the question and prior evidence.

items.title: 177 Lovers and Counting
items.summary: An autoethnography places personal and professional experiences of sex, jealousy and non-monogamy within changing American sexual cultures over several decades.

items.title: Implicit Attitudes to Parents and Romantic Partners
items.summary: Reports that the college students studied tended to evaluate their parental relationships more positively than their romantic relationships.

items.title: Love for a Partner and a Musical Instrument
items.summary: Uses music education students’ accounts to examine love directed at both people and objects. Reads their experiences through love and self-expansion theories.

items.title: Affectionate Touch and Romantic Love
items.summary: Across the samples, stronger love predicted more frequent and varied affectionate touch. The abstract reports convergence across a cross-cultural study and a second, more homogeneous sample.

items.title: The Power of Love
items.summary: Conceptualises love as a disposition with potential and actual expressions. A disposition can exist between its visible manifestations.

items.title: Why Study Love Worldwide?
items.summary: Reports cross-cultural support for the intimacy, passion and commitment framework and asks which social and environmental conditions explain variations in its expression.

items.title: African Othellos and Desdemonas
items.summary: Reads Sudanese fiction alongside Othello to examine how jealous love and its alternatives become ways of thinking about migration and postcolonial identity.

items.title: Fifty Shades as a Guide to Love, Sex and Eroticism
items.summary: Interprets the novels as a vehicle for fantasy and sexual self-exploration. The argument concerns reading and popular reception.

items.title: Love and Desire among Chinese Migrants in Kingston
items.summary: Ethnography treats love as something experienced in everyday atmosphere, gestures and silences. Migration shapes how attachment is felt and communicated.

items.title: Posthuman Eroticism and Erobots
items.summary: Proposes that erotic technologies change how desire and human–machine relations are understood, with humans and technologies shaping one another over time.

items.title: Being in Love with Others
items.summary: Reads Dworkin and Fanon to ask how authentic intimacy can recognise the distinct person while accounting for social power and oppression.

items.title: Marsilio Ficino’s Erotic Hedonism
items.summary: Challenges a sharp break between Ficino’s early interest in pleasure and later philosophy. Argues that he located happiness in the pleasure of loving God and divine providence.

items.title: Polyamory and Monogamy in Romance Novels
items.summary: Examines how recently published romances diversify their relationship scripts and asks what expanding beyond the soulmate couple reveals about changing cultural expectations.

items.title: Relationship-driven Self-change and Authenticity
items.summary: In a sample of 253 people, self-expansion and self-contraction were important predictors of feeling authentic in the relationship. Feeling diminished was particularly relevant to felt deception.

items.title: Love as a Creative Force
items.summary: Examines how metaphors of love as a force can connect creation, sacred understandings and women’s roles in traditional communities.

items.title: Red Flags and Inclusion of Other in the Self
items.summary: In a dating-profile study, stronger perceived identity overlap made prospective partners more desirable and negative behaviours seem less serious. The reported effect persisted over two days.

items.title: Pedagogical Love in Sámi Curatorial Education
items.summary: Uses a two-year programme to examine how care, compassion and empathy can inform Indigenous curatorial training and educational design.

items.title: Divine Love and Causation in Ibn Sina and Aristotle
items.summary: Compares Aristotle’s mover with Ibn Sina’s Necessary Existent and argues that both serve as a final goal towards which love moves the cosmos.

items.title: Love Metaphors in Dementia
items.summary: Explores how people with dementia express love through metaphor. The findings suggest that conceptual and emotional importance can persist amid changes in language.

items.title: Self-Love and Selfhood
items.summary: Develops a Kierkegaardian account of self-love as willing to be oneself and uses it to distinguish different ways of relating to one’s own identity.

items.title: Emotional Work in Young Danes’ Digitised Dating Lives
items.summary: Proposes long-term ethnographic attention to the emotional labour involved in dating apps, including how people retell encounters and adopt practices they previously resisted.

items.title: Isolation, Belonging and Belief in Incel Communities
items.summary: Uses Iris Murdoch’s idea of loving attention to explore how exclusion and belonging can shape people’s relationship to evidence, other people and conspiracy narratives.

items.title: Discourses of Love, Sacrifice and Selfishness in South Korea
items.summary: Survey responses differ by gender on sacrifice and the material conditions of relationships. Nelson links these patterns to changing gender expectations and pressures on men to provide.

items.title: Maintaining Sexual Intimacy While Living Apart Together Transnationally
items.summary: Most couples in the study sustained intimacy across national borders. Memories, digital communication and sometimes sexual contact by phone or online helped maintain connection.

items.title: Kyoto School Philosophy on the Nature of Love
items.summary: Compares several philosophical views of loving as experiencing the world with another person, being conscious of them or seeing through their perspective.

items.title: How South Asian Multigenerational Families Communicate Love in Elder Care
items.summary: Research on migrant families in California examines how everyday care can express love through duty. It also asks how several generations negotiate burdens and disagreements while living together.

items.title: Stance Without Connection: Email in Elif Batuman’s The Idiot
items.summary: The programme lists a literary study of how email communication expresses stance and relates to interpersonal connection in the novel. The programme does not state the findings.

items.title: Intentions and Interpretations of I Love You
items.summary: In a Southern California student sample, the expression most often conveyed intimacy, then commitment and then sexual desire. The relative meanings varied by gender and, to a lesser extent, ethnicity and immigrant generation.

items.title: Sibling Identity Overlap as a Predictor of Flourishing
items.summary: The presentation examines whether sharing a sense of identity with a sibling predicts flourishing. The programme does not state the direction or size of the relationship.

items.title: Family Bonds and Roles in It Takes Two
items.summary: Dialogue and cooperative gameplay turn family repair into an active process. The authors argue that coordination and communication let players enact what the characters have to learn.

items.title: Chinese Love Influencers on BiliBili
items.authors: Yuhan Su; Zizhen Wang; Kyungmin Kim; Alex Nelson; Yeon Jung Yu; Yura Park
items.summary: A content analysis of romantic relationship advice given by BiliBili influencers. The programme identifies the study and research team but does not report results.

items.title: Korean Love Influencers on YouTube
items.authors: Yura Park; Kyungmin Kim; Alex Nelson; Yeon Jung Yu; Yuhan Su
items.summary: A content analysis of relationship advice given by Korean YouTube influencers. The programme lists the study but provides no findings.

items.title: Canarian-set popular romance and Spanish language
items.summary: Studies English-language romances set in the Canary Islands and other Atlantic islands. The project examines how the novels represent cultural difference and circulate Spanish words and phrases among international readers.

items.title: Love and Relationship Satisfaction Across Relationship Stages
items.summary: Across relationship stages in a Brazilian cross-sectional sample, passion and intimacy had stronger associations with satisfaction at later stages, while the association with commitment weakened.
